text: Multiple categories of cases involved: (1) End-users purchasing shrink-wrapped software directly from foreign suppliers; (2) Indian distributors purchasing from foreign suppliers and reselling to Indian end-users; (3) Foreign distributors selling to Indian distributors/end-users; (4) Software embedded in hardware sold as integrated units. The key fact common to all categories is that under the EULAs and distribution agreements, no copyright or copyright rights were transferred to the distributors or end-users—only a limited right to use the software was granted, with no right to reproduce, sublicense, or transfer. The distributors had no right to use the software themselves and merely resold sealed copies to end-users for profit.

text: The payments do not constitute royalty. Royalty requires transfer of all or any rights in copyright (including granting of licence in which copyright interest passes). Under the EULAs/distribution agreements in these cases, only right to use software is granted; no copyright rights are transferred.. Article 12(3) of DTAA defines royalties as payments for 'use of, or the right to use, any copyright' of literary work. Section 9(1)(vi) Explanation 2(v) defines royalty as consideration for 'transfer of all or any rights (including granting of licence) in respect of any copyright.' Copyright is exclusive right under section 14 of Copyright Act to do acts such as reproduce, issue copies, translate, adapt. Ownership of copyright is distinct from ownership of physical material (copyrighted article). Purchaser of book/CD becomes owner of physical article but not copyright. Here, distributors received no rights to reproduce, sublicense, or transfer software—only right to use shrink-wrapped sealed copies. No parting with copyright occurred. Courts must distinguish between copyright (exclusive right to reproduce, adapt, etc.) and copyrighted article (physical manifestation). EULA restrictions and non-exclusive, non-transferable character confirm no copyright transfer. Mere copying necessary for operation under section 52(1)(aa) of Copyright Act does not constitute infringement and thus does not represent transfer of copyright. Therefore, transaction amounts to sale of goods (copyrighted article), not royalty.

text: No obligation to deduct TDS arose. Section 195(1) requires deduction only on 'sums chargeable under the provisions of this Act.' Since payments were not for royalty and did not give rise to income taxable in India under section 9, no deduction was required.. Section 195(1) is inextricably linked with charging provision in section 9(1)(vi) read with section 4. TDS obligation exists only if non-resident is liable to pay tax under charging provision. Words 'chargeable under the provisions of [the] Act' in section 195(1) are critical—tax deductible only from income actually chargeable under sections 4, 5, and 9. GE Technology case correctly held that moment remittance occurs does not automatically create TDS obligation; income must be chargeable. Since payments here were for goods (copyrighted articles) and not royalty, no income chargeable in India arose under section 9(1)(vi). Consequence: no TDS deduction obligation. This interpretation accords with principle of proportionality in section 195(2)—deduction limited to 'appropriate proportion' of chargeable sum. Charging and machinery provisions must work in tandem.

text: No copyright is transferred. EULA licence is not licence under section 30 of Copyright Act. It imposes restrictive conditions for use but does not grant interest in any of the exclusive rights contained in section 14(a) and (b) of Copyright Act.. Section 30 of Copyright Act permits owner to grant interest in rights by licence. Such licence transfers interest in exclusive rights (reproduce, issue copies, adapt, etc.). EULA licence differs fundamentally—it merely permits use of product with restrictions. Parties to EULA expressly state copyright remains with owner; licensee gets no right to reproduce beyond what necessary for operation. Section 52(1)(aa) of Copyright Act recognizes that copying/adaptation necessary for utilization is not infringement. This indicates such copying does not represent transfer of copyright right. Difference between 'right to use' copyrighted product and 'right to use copyright' in product is crucial. Former does not transfer copyright; latter does. Under EULAs here, only former transfer occurs. Non-exclusive, non-transferable character shows licensee never divests licensor of copyright rights—licensor retains full control. Therefore, EULA is not licence in terms of Copyright Act section 30.

text: Doctrine of first sale/principle of exhaustion applies to computer software under section 14(b)(ii) of Copyright Act as amended in 1999. After copyright owner's first sale of copy of software, owner's distribution right is exhausted in relation to that copy.. Prior to 1999 Amendment, section 14(b)(ii) read: 'to sell or give on hire...any copy of computer programme, regardless of whether such copy has been sold or given on hire on earlier occasions.' 1999 Amendment deleted phrase 'regardless of whether such copy has been sold on earlier occasions.' This deletion is statutory recognition of doctrine of exhaustion. Explanation to section 14 states: 'a copy which has been sold once shall be deemed to be a copy already in circulation.' Copyright owner's distribution right extends only to copies not already in circulation. Once first sale by owner or with owner's consent, that right is exhausted for subsequent sales of same copy. In these cases, shrink-wrapped copies were put in circulation by foreign suppliers, then distributed by Indian distributors to end-users. These were copies 'already in circulation.' Therefore, distributor's sale/resale did not violate copyright owner's distribution right under section 14(b)(ii). This supports conclusion that distribution is of goods, not transfer of copyright.

text: Explanation 4 cannot apply to assessment years prior to 2012 when provision was not on statute book. Maxim lex non cogit ad impossibilia applies—law does not compel impossible acts. Person responsible for TDS deduction cannot be expected to apply definition that did not factually exist at time of payment/deduction.. Finance Act 2012 inserted Explanation 4 with retrospective effect from 1.6.1976, clarifying that transfer of rights for 'use or right to use' computer software constitutes royalty. However, before Explanation 4 was enacted, this expanded definition did not exist. Similarly, Explanation 3 (defining 'computer software') was first introduced in 1991, much after 1976. Moreover, technology referenced (satellite transmission, optic fibre) was not regulated by Parliament until Cable TV Regulation Act, 1995. For assessment years in question (prior to 2012), expanded definition did not exist. Courts have recognized that person cannot be held liable for non-compliance with provision not in force at relevant time. High Court of Bombay applied maxim in CIT v. NGC Networks, holding parties cannot perform impossible act of complying with provision introduced later by retrospective amendment. Therefore, assessees cannot be held in default for not deducting tax on definition of royalty that did not exist at time of payment.
